newsitem.title: CHINA: China aims to boost sagging car market.
newsitem.headline: China aims to boost sagging car market.

text.p: China announced on Friday an end to local restrictions on the use of small passenger cars in an attempt to combat protectionism by regional authorities and revive sagging car sales.
The State Planning Commission (SPC) issued a notice cancelling restrictions by local governments on the use of "economy cars" to fight regional protectionism, the Economic Daily News said.
"Regional protectionism ... does not conform to the pattern of the market economy," it said. "If this development continued, it will not benefit the whole situation."
The move also aims to boost the development of the domestic car industry, the newspaper added.
Industry officials say local authorities in some parts of China restrict sales of small passenger cars not made in their region to promote sales of locally made vehicles.

"Local governments use the excuse of traffic congestion to limit car use," an official of the SPC in Beijing said by telephone. "What they should do is improve the traffic situation, not restrict car buying."

She said the notice applied to three kinds of cars, all with engines below one litre -- the Charade made in the eastern city of Tianjin, the Alto produced in the southwest city of Chongqing and the Skylark made in the southwest city of Guiyang.
She criticised restrictions introduced by the city governments in Shanghai and Beijing.

As from February in Beijing, jeeps, light buses and sedans with engines smaller than one litre and carrying licence plates beginning with an odd number are limited to driving only on odd-numbered days. The same applies to vehicles with even-numbered plates.

"These restrictions were unreasonable and unsuitable for the market economy," the SPC official said. "This was the view of a certain senior leader who passed it to the State Planning Commission. We at the SPC also believe this regulation to be unreasonable," she said.
She also described as "unreasonable" a regulation by the Shanghai city government to gradually ban the use of Charades as taxis, with such taxis to be banned by the end of 1997.
Shanghai says that the Charade is too small and of too poor quality for an international city, but critics say the move is aimed at promoting sales of locally made Santanas as taxis.

The SPC official also described as unreasonable the auctions of car licences by some cities as a way to discourage car ownership. She declined to say if Friday's regulations make these measures illegal.

China's car market is in a slump, with production racing ahead of demand. In the first half of 1996, China produced 758,000 automobiles, up 2.42 percent compared with the same period last year, while sales dropped by 0.1 percent to 720,000 units, official figures show.

Stockpiles of automobiles rose to 116,000 units in June from 88,000 units earlier this year, with stockpiles of sedan cars reaching 19,600 units, rising 233.7 percent from the same period last year, the figures showed.
China produced 1.503 million motor vehicles in 1995, up 10 percent from 1994, and plans to manufacture 2.7 million in the year 2000. It wants to turn auto manufacturing into a pillar industry.
